summary: Defines pre-shared key cipher suites for TLS that use stronger hashes (SHA-256 or SHA-384) and AES in Galois Counter Mode. Earlier PSK suites in RFC 4279 and RFC 4785 relied on SHA-1 in their message authentication code, so this gives newer options.

eli5.summary: Two friends who already share a secret can use it to lock their messages. This note adds newer, stronger locks that work with a pre-shared secret and are harder to break than the older ones.

subtitle: Eighteen new TLS cipher suites that pair a pre-shared key with SHA-256/384 and AES in Galois Counter Mode.

tldr.problem: The existing pre-shared key cipher suites for TLS in RFC 4279 and RFC 4785 all use HMAC-SHA1, and the IETF was moving away from SHA-1 after new analytic work on it.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines six AES-GCM suites that use authenticated encryption, plus twelve suites that keep the old PSK key exchanges but swap SHA-1 for SHA-256 or SHA-384 in the MAC and PRF.
tldr.outcome: Systems that authenticate with pre-shared keys get cipher suites built on stronger hashes. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 10015.

today: RFC 5487 is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 10015. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why New PSK Cipher Suites
sections.content:
A pre-shared key (PSK) cipher suite lets two TLS endpoints authenticate each other with a symmetric secret they already hold, instead of public/private key pairs. The benefits of that approach are explained in the introduction of RFC 4279; this document reuses those key exchanges and only upgrades the cryptographic building blocks.

Two things drive the upgrade. First, TLS 1.2 (RFC 5246) added support for authenticated encryption with additional data (AEAD) cipher modes from RFC 5116. Second, every cipher suite in RFC 4279 and RFC 4785 uses HMAC-SHA1 as its MAC, and, citing recent analytic work on SHA-1, the RFC says the IETF is gradually moving towards stronger hash algorithms.

The RFC points to two related documents for public-key suites, RFC 5288 and RFC 5289, and expects the reader to know them first.
sections.eli5: The old locks used a hash that people had started to find weak spots in. This note brings in better locks that work with the same shared secret.

sections.title: Where the Suites Can Be Used
sections.content:
The RFC splits its suites into two groups, and each group has its own version rule. The suites in Section 3 (the SHA-256/384 ones) can be negotiated whatever the negotiated TLS version is. The suites in Section 2 (the AES-GCM ones) can be negotiated in TLS version 1.2 or higher.

The applicability statement in RFC 4279 applies here as well.
sections.eli5: The newest locks need the newest version of the lock-making rules. The other new locks work with any version.

sections.title: The AES-GCM Suites
sections.content:
Six cipher suites use AES in Galois Counter Mode (AES-GCM), an AEAD mode, together with the PSK, DHE_PSK and RSA_PSK key exchanges. They use the AEAD algorithms AEAD_AES_128_GCM and AEAD_AES_256_GCM from RFC 5116, and GCM is used as described in RFC 5288. The key exchanges themselves are performed as defined in RFC 4279.

The two DHE_PSK suites provide Perfect Forward Secrecy (PFS). The Pseudo-Random Function (PRF) SHALL be the TLS PRF from RFC 5246 with SHA-256 for suites ending in _SHA256, and with SHA-384 for suites ending in _SHA384.

Implementations MUST send a TLS Alert bad_record_mac for all types of failures encountered while processing the AES-GCM algorithm.
sections.eli5: These locks scramble the message and stamp it with a seal in one step. If anything goes wrong opening it, the receiver always shouts the same alarm word.

sections.title: The SHA-256 and SHA-384 Suites
sections.content:
Twelve more suites, spread across the PSK, DHE_PSK and RSA_PSK key exchanges, copy the matching suites from RFC 4279 and RFC 4785 and change only the hash and PRF. Within each key exchange, the first two use AES in Cipher Block Chaining (CBC) mode for confidentiality (AES-128 with SHA-256, AES-256 with SHA-384). The other two use NULL encryption, so they give integrity protection and authentication but no confidentiality.

For names ending in _SHA256 or _SHA384, the MAC is HMAC (RFC 2104) with SHA-256 or SHA-384 as the hash. When negotiated in a TLS version before 1.2, the PRF of that version is used. Otherwise, the PRF is the TLS PRF with the same hash.

Only the PSK suites are spelled out in Section 3.1. The DHE_PSK and RSA_PSK sections say they work the same way, with the same hash and PRF changes.
sections.eli5: These keep the old lock design but swap the stamp-maker for a stronger one. Some versions skip scrambling and only stamp the message.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 4279, RFC 4785 and RFC 5288 apply to this document too.

The authentication-only suites with NULL encryption do not support confidentiality. Care should be taken not to send sensitive information, such as passwords, over connections protected with one of them.
sections.eli5: Some of these locks only prove who sent the message and do not hide it. Never put a secret in a message that is not hidden.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: IANA assigned a two-byte value to each of the eighteen suites, all starting with 0x00. The AES-GCM suites take 0xA8 to 0xAD. The SHA-256/384 suites take 0xAE to 0xB9, in the order PSK, DHE_PSK and RSA_PSK, with AES-128 CBC, AES-256 CBC, NULL SHA256 and NULL SHA384 in each group.
sections.eli5: Each new lock gets its own number so both sides can say which one they want.
